Agentic Design Patterns

From simple loops to multi-step planning. How agents structure their execution flow to solve tasks.

1. ReAct (Reason + Act)

The foundational pattern for agents (Yao et al., 2022). It interleaves Reasoning (Thought) and Acting (Tool calls). Instead of just acting blindly, the agent "thinks" about what to do next, executes it, observes the output, and repeats.

graph TD Start --> Thought1["Thought: I need to search for weather"] Thought1 --> Action1["Action: Search(City)"] Action1 --> Obs1["Observation: 25°C, Sunny"] Obs1 --> Thought2["Thought: Now I can answer"] Thought2 --> Ans["Final Answer"] style Thought1 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#818cf8 style Action1 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#eab308 style Obs1 fill:#1e293b,stroke:#22c55e

2. Plan-and-Execute

For complex tasks, ReAct can get lost in the weeds. Plan-and-Execute separates the "Planning" phase from the "Execution" phase.

  • Planner: Decomposes the user request into a list of steps.
  • Executor: Executes each step, potentially using a ReAct loop for each one.
  • Replanner: (Optional) Updates the plan based on new information.
graph LR User --> Planner Planner -->|List of Steps| Executor Executor -->|Step 1 done| Executor Executor -->|Step 2 done| Executor Executor -->|All done| Final style Planner fill:#0f172a,stroke:#38bdf8,stroke-width:2px style Executor fill:#1e293b,stroke:#f472b6,stroke-width:2px

Static vs. Dynamic Planning

Static Planning: The plan is fixed at the start (e.g., "1. Search X, 2. Search Y, 3. Compare").
Dynamic Replanning: The agent pauses after every step to check if the remaining plan is still valid. "I found X, but it contradicts my assumption, so I need to delete step 2 and add step 4."
